sections.h2: Where is Franklin, Tennessee, and how fast has it grown?
sections.html:
Franklin is the county seat of Williamson County, about 21 miles south of Nashville on the Harpeth River. It is the seventh-largest city in Tennessee. The Census Bureau lists 62,487 people in 2010, 83,454 in 2020 and 90,226 in its July 2025 estimate, an increase of 8.0 percent over the 2020 base. Land area is 42.75 square miles, or roughly 1,952 residents per square mile at the 2020 count.

Franklin's population is more than five times what it was in 1980, when 12,407 people lived here. That rise came as northern Franklin filled with houses and offices, and as the city became a Nashville suburb with its own jobs. For a homeowner thinking about selling in Franklin, the pace of growth explains why house values here sit well above the national figure.

sections.h2: What in Franklin's history still shows up in its houses?
sections.html:
Abram Maury Jr. founded the town on October 26, 1799, and named it for Benjamin Franklin. The Second Battle of Franklin on November 30, 1864 produced nearly 10,000 casualties and turned forty-four buildings into temporary field hospitals. The Carter, Carnton and Lotz houses from that era still stand.

Five historic districts in the city are listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and Franklin is noted for older buildings and neighborhoods protected by city ordinance. A former stove factory, the Dortch Stove Works of 1928 that later made Magic Chef ranges, was restored in the late 1990s and now holds offices, restaurants and retail space.

Houses near the square or inside a historic district can carry design rules that a suburban subdivision lot does not, so an owner there should ask City Hall what applies before planning repairs.

sections.h2: Which employers and roads support Franklin's housing market?
sections.html:
Franklin has a deep base of health care and corporate employers. The city's 2024 annual financial report, as summarized on Wikipedia, ranks the top ten employers, and the largest are below.

Interstate 65 crosses the eastern side of the city with four exits, and US 31 and US 431 run together toward Nashville. State Routes 96, 246 and 441 fan out from Franklin, and the Mack Hatcher Parkway bypass circles the business district to the east. Cool Springs Boulevard and McEwen Drive both have interchanges with I-65.

The city's 2026-27 budget message says a 10-year capital plan of $458 million is 82 percent devoted to transportation, including a state partnership to widen Mack Hatcher Parkway Southeast, the widening of McEwen Road and a new City Hall on the downtown square.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers say about Franklin homes?
sections.html:
QuickFacts for Franklin shows a median owner-occupied home value of $705,400 for 2020 to 2024, against $332,700 for the nation. Median selected owner costs are $2,542 a month with a mortgage and $712 without one. Median gross rent is $1,923. Roughly 63.8 percent of homes are owner-occupied across the city's 33,998 households.

Median household income is $119,528, 64.5 percent of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or higher, and 84.6 percent of residents lived in the same house a year earlier. Those figures describe a market where most owners have stayed put and where the typical house carries a large price tag.

sections.h2: What does a Franklin homeowner pay in property tax?
sections.html:
Franklin's city rate is $0.296 per $100 of assessed value, and the proposed 2026-27 budget leaves it unchanged. The rate has two parts: a $0.2310 base for operations and debt, plus $0.0650 added after the last reappraisal for infrastructure and city services. The city calls its rate one of the lowest in Tennessee. The county assessor reappraises every four years.

The Williamson County Trustee bills for the county, the Franklin Special School District and the city together. Here is how the county's published schedule works:

  • Statements go out in early October.
  • Taxes are payable from the first Monday in October through February 28.
  • Interest of 1.5 percent is added on March 1, and it keeps accruing on the first of each month.
  • The trustee has no authority to waive, prorate or release tax or interest.
  • Bills go to the owner of record on January 1, so a seller who closes mid-year must forward the bill to the new owner.

As an example, a Franklin house assessed at 25 percent of a $700,000 value carries $175,000 of assessed value, and the city share at $0.296 per $100 comes to $518. County and school charges are on top of that, so ask the trustee at 615-790-5709 for the full figure on a specific parcel.

sections.h2: What city fees and utilities will a Franklin buyer ask about?
sections.html:
Buyers often ask about monthly costs, and Franklin's budget documents answer part of the question. Residential trash and recycling is set to rise by $1 to $34 a month in fiscal 2027, and stormwater fees are projected to add about $20.70 a year for most homes. Water and sewer rates rose 6 percent and 5.7 percent on January 1, 2026.

The city's water department serves most residents, though pockets are served by the Mallory Valley, Milcrofton and HB&TS utility districts. Electricity comes from Middle Tennessee Electric through TVA power, and gas from Atmos Energy. A seller should know which provider serves the address before a buyer asks.

sections.h2: Where is a Franklin deed recorded, and what does recording cost?
sections.html:
Deeds for Franklin houses are filed with the Williamson County Register of Deeds at 1320 West Main Street, Suite 201, Franklin, open 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. on weekdays. The office posts a fee calculator and an electronic filing option, and the phone number is 615-790-5706. The county assessor, at 615-790-5708, handles questions about assessed value and the mailing address on a bill.

Recording also triggers state tax. The Tennessee Department of Revenue sets the realty transfer tax at $0.37 per $100 of purchase price, and a buyer's loan adds a mortgage tax of $0.115 per $100 of debt after the first $2,000. The register collects both and forwards them to the state.

Anyone selling a Franklin house for cash, through an agent or on their own should have the title company confirm the payoff, the unpaid taxes and the recording steps before closing day.

faqs.a: Franklin had 83,454 residents in the 2020 census and an estimated 90,226 in July 2025, making it one of the largest cities in Tennessee. It covers about 42.75 square miles of land.

faqs.q: What is Franklin's city property tax rate?
faqs.a: The city rate is $0.296 per $100 of assessed value, and the proposed 2026-27 budget keeps it there. Williamson County and the Franklin Special School District add their own charges on the same bill.

faqs.q: When are Williamson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Taxes are payable from the first Monday in October through February 28. Starting March 1, interest of 1.5 percent applies, and it keeps accruing on the first of each month.

faqs.q: Who pays Tennessee's transfer tax on a Franklin sale?
faqs.a: The grantee, meaning the buyer, pays the realty transfer tax of $0.37 per $100 of purchase price. The Register of Deeds collects it when the deed is recorded.

faqs.q: Which office records a deed for a Franklin house?
faqs.a: The Williamson County Register of Deeds, 1320 West Main Street, Suite 201, handles it. Call 615-790-5706 with questions about recording or the fee calculator.
